list.listitem: Suspect (non-orbital) cellulitis in a patient with acutely expanding erythema, warmth, swelling, and tenderness of the skin.C

Clinical impression, while not highly accurate, remains the best way to diagnose cellulitis in a patient presenting with a red leg. History of prior cellulitis, excoriating skin disorders, obesity, chronic leg swelling, tinea pedis, and unilateral presentation make the diagnosis more likely. Lack of warmth of the affected limb relative to the unaffected extremity decreases the probability of the diagnosis. C

Treat typical cellulitis in an immunocompetent patient without systemic symptoms for at least 5 days with oral antibiotics active against Group A streptococci (Streptococcus pyogenes), such as penicillin, dicloxacillin, cephalexin, or clindamycin. A
Consider coverage for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) in immunocompromised patients or for purulent, complicated, or severe cellulitis. B

Despite adequate treatment of leg cellulitis, some signs and symptoms of inflammation (eg, erythema, edema, warmth, pain) can remain for at least 10 days from treatment initiation and may not indicate treatment failure. B

In adult patients with recurrent cellulitis of the leg (ie, 2 episodes over 3 years), prophylactic penicillin or erythromycin may be effective in preventing recurrence; most adverse events are minor such as nausea and rash.B

background.definition: Cellulitis is an acute, spreading infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue that may be complicating a wound, ulcer, or dermatosis. This topic covers non-orbital cellulitis. See Periorbital and orbital cellulitis for information on that topic.

list.listitem: Incidence rate of cellulitis ranges from 0.2 to 24.6 per 1000 person-years.
Cellulitis is almost always unilateral and typically affects the lower extremity especially in older adults.
Cellulitis or abscess of the leg (excluding the foot) accounted for 5.4% of infectious disease hospitalizations in the US, and the percentage remained similar from 2001-2014.

Nonpurulent, uncomplicated cellulitis in an immunocompetent patient is often attributed to group A streptococci (Streptococcus pyogenes) and to Staphylococcus aureus to a lesser extent. Difficulty in verifying the causative organism through culture has been a challenge in studies evaluating nonpurulent cellulitis. In a systematic review of 808 adults and children with cellulitis who underwent needle aspiration or punch biopsy of intact skin, only 16% grew bacteria in their cultures (51% grew S. aureus, 27% grew S. pyogenes). Although abscesses were excluded in the study, purulent cellulitis was not, which may account for the higher proportion of S. aureus infections. In an inpatient study of 179 (of 248) cases of nonculturable cellulitis, 73% were attributed to β-hemolytic streptococci based on acute and convalescent serologies for antistreptolysin-O and anti-DNase-B antibodies.
Methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) is the most common bacteria isolated from purulent skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs).

Gram-negative organisms are rarely the cause of cellulitis, but should be considered in certain circumstances such as animal bites, aquatic injury, peri-rectal infections, surgical site infections involving the groin or abdominal wall, infections with signs concerning for necrotizing infection, and infections in neutropenic or severely immunocompromised patients.
Auricular chondritis associated with ear piercing may be caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Opportunistic fungal infection is a rare cause of cellulitis but should be considered if cellulitis responds only partially to antibiotic therapy in severely immunocompromised patients.

Mycobacterium marinum is a rare but serious cause of cellultis that can lead to dactylitis or osteomyelitis if left untreated. It should be considered in patients with a nodular rash unreponsive to usual cellulitis treatment and a history of saltwater fish exposure (long incubation period of approximately 21 days).

Cellulitis generally occurs after the protective barrier of the skin, the epidermis, has been compromised (eg, trauma, ulcers, maceration, eczema), allowing bacterial access to the subepidermal tissues.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Presence of S. Aureus and/or β-hemolytic streptococci in the toe webs

list.listitem: In adult patients with recurrent cellulitis of the leg (ie, 2 episodes over 3 years), prophylactic penicillin or erythromycin may be effective in preventing recurrence; most adverse events are minor such as nausea and rash. A
Consider treating lower extremity edema by recommending leg elevation, compression stockings or pneumatic compression devices, and, if appropriate, diuretic therapy. C
Based on a small, single-center, nonblinded trial, compression therapy in patients with chronic leg edema may decrease the incidence of recurrent cellulitis and may be cost-saving. B
Measures to modify local risk for cellulitis, such as treating interdigital maceration and keeping skin well hydrated with emollients to avoid dryness and cracking, may reduce recurrence. C
Suspect cellulitis in a patient with acutely expanding erythema, warmth, swelling, and tenderness of the skin. C

Misdiagnosis rate for cellulitis is approximately 40% (range 19-83%) in outpatient and inpatient settings with the majority of misdiagnoses attributed to non-infectious causes (eg, stasis dermatitis, eczematous dermatitis, and edema/lymphedema). B

Clinical impression, while not highly accurate, remains the best way to diagnose cellulitis in a patient presenting with a red leg. History of prior cellulitis, excoriating skin disorders, obesity, chronic leg swelling, tinea pedis, and unilateral presentation make the diagnosis more likely. Lack of warmth of the affected limb relative to the unaffected extremity decreases the probability of the diagnosis. C
For mild typical cellulitis, do not routinely perform labs (eg, CBC, blood culture, superficial swab/culture) or imaging. C
Consider point-of-care ultrasonography (POCUS) to differentiate cellulitis from abscess. It is particularly accurate and superior than clinical exam in ruling out abscess. A

While newer approaches like thermal imaging, clinical prediction models (eg, ALT-70, New HAvUN), computer-aided decision support tools, and point-of-care tests (eg, procalcitonin) may improve diagnostic accuracy, evidence is very limited to support their routine use in primary care. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Bilateral hyperpigmented patches of the legs with xerosis and sometimes chronic erythema
Erythema and other cutaneous findings at site of allergen contact, without signs of systemic illness
Painless, progressive, bilateral limb swelling that is sometimes asymmetric; associated with non-pitting edema and skin fibrosis at later stages
Well demarcated, warm, tender, fiery red plaque involving the face, penis, or extremities, usually preceded by systemic symptoms and associated with lymphadenopathy
Skin is not generally involved, but swelling, pain, and erythema can be present
Warm, erythematous patches and plaques overlying tender cord (vein)
Early skin findings may be subtle (eg, edema, erythema), but pain is usually disproportionate to clinical findings and may rapidly evolve to formation of bullae, ecchymoses, and skin necrosis.
Onset of local erythema, itching, increased warmth, and sometimes pain and swelling 1-3 days after an insect bite
Dependent rubor that resolves with elevation; associated with diminished or absent pedal pulses
Tender, erythematous, subcutaneous nodules and plaques of the shin that may be associated with connective tissue disease
Acute monoarticular inflammation that may be associated with erythema, warmth, swelling and tenderness of overlying skin
Acute onset of erythema, warmth, and swelling of foot and/or ankle, with or without pain, associated with foot/ankle deformity, among persons with diabetes
Seen in immunocompromised patients; appears similar to bacterial cellulitis, but only modestly improves with antibiotic treatment

list.listitem: Cellulitis presents as acutely expanding erythema, warmth, swelling, and tenderness of the skin. Unlike erysipelas, the erythema associated with cellulitis does not have sharply demarcated borders. Lymphangitic streaking and regional lymphadenopathy are usually present in erysipelas but may be less common in cellulitis.

Given the lack of specificity of cellulitis signs and symptoms, the misdiagnosis rate for cellulitis in meta-analyses is approximately 40% (range 19-83%) in outpatient and inpatient settings with the majority of misdiagnoses attributed to non-infectious causes (eg, stasis dermatitis, eczematous dermatitis, and edema/lymphedema).

Unilateral signs and symptoms paired with a suggestive history increase the likelihood of cellulitis, but there is no definitive way to differentiate cellulitis from other causes of a red leg. Historical elements that increase the likelihood of cellulitis include previous cellulitis, lymphedema or chronic leg edema, excoriating skin disorders, tinea pedis, and BMI >30. Lack of warmth of the affected limb relative to the unaffected extremity decreases the probability of the diagnosis.

The skin surface may resemble an orange peel (ie, peau d'orange) because superficial cutaneous edema surrounds hair follicles, causing dimpling in the skin due to the hair connection to the underlying dermis.
Systemic symptoms, such as fever, chills, and general malaise, may also be present in severe cases.

Clinical findings suggesting potentially severe, deep soft tissue infection (ie, necrotizing fasciitis) include the following: (1) pain disproportionate to the physical findings, (2) violaceous bullae, (3) cutaneous hemorrhage, (4) skin sloughing, (5) skin anesthesia, (6) rapid progression, and (7) gas in the tissue. In Fournier's gangrene, a prodromal period of perineal swelling for up to 3 weeks often is present.

An analysis of 259 inpatients initially diagnosed with cellulitis, of whom 79 were felt to have been misdiagnosed and had another cause, concluded that asymmetry, leukocytosis, tachycardia, and age ≥70 years were the strongest independent predictors of cellulitis as the true diagnosis.
Laboratory investigation, including needle aspiration, CBC, and diagnostic imaging is of limited value for mild to moderate cellulitis.
If the skin is broken and there is risk of uncommon pathogens (eg, penetrating trauma, exposure to water-borne pathogens, or travel), consider taking a swab for microbiological testing.

For patients with soft tissue infection accompanied by signs and symptoms of systemic toxicity (eg, fever or hypothermia, tachycardia [heart rate >100 beats/min], and hypotension [systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg or 20 mm Hg below baseline]), consider the following laboratory studies: CBC with differential, creatinine, bicarbonate, creatine phosphokinase, lactate, CRP, and blood culture.

Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) has good diagnostic accuracy for differentiating abscess from cellulitis. A meta-analysis of 14 studies showed POCUS was 94.6% sensitive and 85.4% specific, with a LR+ of 6.5 and LR− of 0.06 and resulted in a correct change in managment in 10% of cases. Accuracy was better for adults (LR+ 10.9, LR- 0.01) than for children (LR+ 4.5, LR- 0.13) and better among cases with high pretest suspicion for abscess or cellulitis (LR+ 8.6, LR- 0.07) than for those that were clinically unclear (LR+ 4.0, LR- 0.11). POCUS is particularly helpful in ruling out abscesses and outperforms physical exam alone.

Temperature differences between an area of suspected cellulitis and the contralateral side, measured by thermal imaging with a smart phone attachment, can increase diagnostic accuracy for uncomplicated cellulitis in the ED. A temperature difference of 0.47 ºC or greater between affected and unaffected skin had 96.6% sensitivity, 45.5% specificity, 82.4% positive predictive value, and 83.3% negative predictive value for cellulitis diagnosis. Validation of this model showed an 87.5% accuracy in cellulitis diagnosis compared to the typical 70% diagnostic accuracy. Similarly, a skin surface temperature difference of ≥0.8 ºC between the affected area and the contralateral side, measured by an inexpensive handheld infrared thermometer, had 95% sensitivity and 69% specificity for diagnosis of cellulitis in 52 patients referred to infectious disease specialists with suspected cellulitis.

A single-center prospective trial compared effectiveness of various thermal imaging measures with a thermal camera attached to an ipad in diagnosing cellulitis in patients coming to the emergency department with acute lower extremity dermatology symptoms including erythema. The maximum skin surface temperature outperformed the mean temperature and the temperature gradients between affected and unaffected side for both the maxiumum and mean temperatures. A maximum skin surface temperature of the affected area of ≥31.2 ºC had a sensitivity of 96.8%, specificity of 38.8%, negative predictive value of 93.5%, and positive predictive value of 57.1% for cellulitis diagnosis.

ALT-70 is a prospectively validated tool to help differentiate between lower extremity cellulitis and pseudocellulitis (conditions that mimic cellulitis) at the time of ED presentation or at 24 and 48 hours after ED presentation. Points are awarded for asymmetry (+3), leukocytosis ≥10,000/μL (+1), tachycardia ≥90 bpm (+1), and age ≥70 years (+2). An ALT-70 score of 0-2 points indicated ≥83.3% likelihood of pseudocellulitis. Whereas, an ALT-70 score ≥5 conferred a positive predictive value for cellulitis ≥82.2% in the ED and at 24 hours, and 84.9% at 48 hours. Comparisons between performace of the ALT-70 clinical prediction rule and thermal imaging (difference in temperature between affected and unaffected sides vs. maximum temperature) have been mixed.A single-center prospective trial compared effectiveness of ALT-70, various thermal imaging measures with a thermal camera attached to an ipad, and a combination of those measures in diagnosing cellulitis in patients coming to the emergency department with acute lower extremity dermatology symptoms including erythema. All measures had sensitivity above 90% although an ALT-70 score ≥ 3 had higher sensitivity and negative predictive value (98.8% and 95.2%, respectively) than the most effective thermal imaging (maximum skin surface temperature ≥31.2 ºC; 93.5% and 87.8% ) or the combination (91.7% and 87.5%). The combination measure had improved specificity and positive predictive value (53.9% and 64.7%, respectively) over either ALT-70 (22.0% and 53.9%) or thermal imaging (38.4% and 55.5%) alone. The maximum skin surface temperature may be used alone or in combination with ALT-70 to reduce overdiagnosis of cellulitis and unnecessary antibiotic use.

In a small retrospective cohort study, presence of 4 out of 7 NEW HAvUN criteria, consisting of new onset, erythema, warmth/fever, history of trauma, ache, unilaterality, and number of white cells, resulted in 100% sensitivity and 95% specificity in differentiating cellulitis from stasis dermatitis or lipodermatosclerosis.

To guide use of intravenous (IV) versus oral antibiotics, the Melbourne ASSET Score was derived and validated in a prospective cohort study of children presenting to the ED with cellulitis using the actual route of administration 24 hours later as the standard. Points are awarded for area (+1 for ≥1% body surface area), systemic features (+1), swelling (+1 for mild, +2 for moderate to severe), eye involvement (+1), and tenderness (+1 for mild, +2 for moderate to severe) with a maximum score of 7. A score of 4 or higher predicted need for IV antibiotics and resulted in 80% correct classification of patients (sensitivity 60%, specificity 93%). Prospective validation of the score yielded an area under the curve of 0.83 (95% CI 0.78-0.89).
The diagnosis of cellulitis is based on clinical findings.
Laboratory investigation including needle aspiration, CBC, and diagnostic imaging is of limited value for mild to moderate cellulitis.
Consider DVT in the differential diagnosis.
Purulence makes MRSA the most likely pathogen.
Consider drawing a line around the extent of the erythema with a single-use surgical marker to monitor progress.

Given the natural history of persistent local inflammatory signs and symptoms during early treatment of mild to moderate lower extremity cellulitis, do not routinely schedule early follow-up visits (48-72 hours) or intensify antibiotic therapy unless symptoms are worsening.

Treat typical cellulitis without systemic symptoms in an immunocompetent patient for 5 days with a single oral antibiotic active against Group A streptococci (Streptococcus pyogenes), such as penicillin, dicloxacillin, cephalexin, or clindamycin. A
Consider coverage for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) in immunocompromised patients or for purulent, complicated, or severe cellulitis. B

Outpatient therapy is recommended unless patients have SIRS, altered mental status or hemodynamic instability, are severely immunocompromised, have poor adherence to therapy, are worsening with appropriate outpatient therapy, or there is concern for deeper or necrotizing infection. C
Use of the validated Melbourne ASSET Score may help guide the choice of oral versus IV antibiotics in children presenting to the ED based on a small, single center, prospective cohort study. B

Typical cellulitis should be treated with an antibiotic active against streptococci. Appropriate choices include penicillin, amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, dicloxacillin, cephalexin, or clindamycin for non-purulent cellulitis that does not require inpatient care.

A systematic review of 43 RCTs evaluating the treatment of nonsurgically-acquired cellulitis found no evidence to support the use of one antibiotic regimen over another. There was no difference for penicillin vs cephalosporins, older vs newer cephalosporins, β-lactams vs macrolides, lincosamide, or streptogramin, linezolid vs other antibiotic, clindamycin vs trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), or quinolone or vancomycin vs other antibiotics. Combination therapy did not improve outcomes over monotherapy even when the combination added MRSA coverage in areas with high community prevalence of MRSA. There is a lack of evidence supporting the use of IV antibiotics over oral antibiotics, or for treatment regimens longer than 5 days. Similarly, data extracted from a multi-center randomized clinical trial found clinical recovery was not improved with antibiotic treatment for more than five days or use of IV rather than oral route for similar severity of cellulitis.
An expanded systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 studies, also found no evidence of difference in clinical responses based on length or route of antibiotic treatment.
An older Cochrane Review of 25 RCTs was unable to define the best treatment for cellulitis, noting the limitations of small, single trials.
Mupirocin 2% cream is an option for minor wound infections; in a study of 706 patients it was as effective as cephalexin 250 mg orally 4 times daily.

MRSA is an uncommon cause of nonpurulent cellulitis, but coverage for MRSA may be sensible for patients with purulent drainage, penetrating trauma, or evidence of concurrent MRSA infection elsewhere. Suitable therapy for MRSA in these situations includes PO doxycycline, TMP-SMX, linezolid, or clindamycin (if clindamycin resistance <10-15% at the institution), as well as IV vancomycin, daptomycin, linezolid, ceftaroline, or telavancin.
Adding TMP-SMX (for MRSA coverage) to cephalexin does not improve cure rates for uncomplicated, nonpurulent cellulitis.

Vancomycin and linezolid are effective in the treatment of complicated skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs) caused by suspected or proven MRSA.Tedizolid has similar efficacy as linezolid in treating cellulitis.
IV daptomycin, a lipopeptide with activity against Gram-positive cocci, appears comparable to vancomycin, linezolid, and tigecycline for the treatment of complicated SSTIs caused by MRSA.
Oral omadacycline once daily is non-inferior to oral linezolid twice daily for acute bacterial SSTIs.

IV dalbavancin in 2 doses (given a week apart) is non-inferior to IV vancomycin (first 3 days) transitioned to PO linezolid (total of 14 days of therapy) for the treatment of acute bacterial SSTIs. Dalbavancin had lower mortality than vancomycin plus linezolid (0.2% vs 1.1%; P = .03).

For complicated and acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections (ABSSI), which include complicated cellulitis, delafloxacin (novel fluoroquinolone with broad antibacterial activity) performed significantly better than fusidic acid, iclaprim, vancomycin, and ceftobiprole for composite clinical response in a network meta-analysis.

Home treatment with IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg once daily was non-inferior to IV flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg every 6 hours in the hospital for children with moderate to severe cellulitis requiring IV antibiotic with no evidence of increase in antibiotic resistance. Home treatment was cost effective.

In terms of efficacy and safety in the outpatient or inpatient settings, a single 1500 mg dose of IV dalbavancin was equivalent to a 1000 mg dose followed by a 500 mg dose one week later. The single-dose regimen had a high degree of patient satisfaction.

Gram-negative organisms are rarely the cause of cellulitis, but antibiotic coverage for these organisms is indicated in certain circumstances such as animal bites, aquatic injury, peri-rectal infections, surgical site infections involving the groin or abdominal wall, infections with signs concerning for necrotizing infection, and infections in neutropenic or severely immunocompromised patients.
Weak evidence supports the use of systemic corticosteroids as adjunctive treatment of cellulitis in adults without diabetes.

At a large pediatric hospital in the US, only 60% of visits to the emergency department or urgent care for non-purulent cellulitis were treated with IDSA guideline-adherent antibiotic treatment, with the most common non-adherence reason being use of clindamycin without documentation of MRSA risk factors (57%). There was no significant association of reutilization rate (3.0% overall) with adherence status in this study.

Rates of guideline-appropriate antibiotic choice and duration for uncomplicated SSTIs for pediatric patients discharged from emergency departments and urgent cares improved from median of 28% to 64% for purulent SSTIs and from 2% to 43% for nonpurulent SSTIs with a revised guideline, discharge order set, and maintenance of certification QI project that included three education sessions and group/individual feedback with no change in the revisitation rate (<2%).
Incision and drainage (I&D) is the initial management of purulent SSTIs like cutaneous furuncle, carbuncle, and abscess.

An early RCT found no additional benefit to adding cephalexin after I&D of skin abscess. However, two newer RCTs suggest that adding MRSA coverage using TMP-SMX or clindamycin after I&D of small, superficial abscesses in children and adults improved cure rates but led to more gastrointestinal adverse events.
Elevation of the affected area may promote drainage of edema and inflammatory substances.

Patients should receive appropriate therapy for any underlying condition that may have predisposed the infection such as peripheral edema, venous insufficiency, venous stasis dermatitis, eczema, diabetes, tinea pedis, or trauma.

Patients with SIRS, altered mental status, hemodynamic instability, concern for deeper or necrotizing infection, poor adherence to therapy, worsening despite appropriate outpatient therapy, or severe immunocompromise warrant admission to the hospital and administration of parenteral antibiotics. Otherwise, stable patients requiring IV antibiotics can be safely treated at home.

Consider referral or hospitalization for children under 1 year of age, older frail individuals with underlying conditions, those who could have uncommon pathogens (eg, penetrating injury, exposure to water-borne organisms, or travel), and those with spreading infections not responding to oral antibiotics.

Early consultation with dermatology may improve diagnostic accuracy, may shorten length of IV antibiotic use, and may result in a higher 2-week improvement rate. Length of hospital stay is not shortened. However, given the lack of a reference standard for diagnosis of cellulitis and poor study descriptions of how dermatologists definitively diagnose cellulitis in clinical trials, it is unclear if early referral to dermatology should be routinely recommended.
Obtain early surgical consultation if necrotizing fasciitis is suspected.

In patients who become increasingly ill, experience increasing toxicity, or in whom deeper infection is suspected, an aggressive evaluation should be initiated and antibiotic treatment should be modified based on Gram stain and culture results as well as antimicrobial susceptibilities of organisms obtained from surgical specimens.

IV antibiotics, rather than oral antibiotics, should be started along with supportive measures for patients who are severely ill, unable to tolerate oral treatment, or where oral treatment would not result in adequate tissue penetration. Patients should be reassessed every 48 hours to determine suitability for switching antibiotics from IV to oral route.

Audits comparing current practice with international guidelines for hospitalized patients with nonpurulent cellulitis show less-than-ideal adherence to guidelines, suggesting the need for development and implementation of evidence-based guidelines at local institutions to improve antibiotic stewardship. A multi-center study of multiple infectious diseases in Switzerland showed only 25% adherence to the recommended duration of antibiotic therapy of 5-7 days for cellulitis. In an audit done in Ireland, 35% of admissions were deemed inappropriate and dual antibiotic therapy was instituted in 96% of cases wheras monotherapy is recommended by IDSA guidelines.

In a study of hospitalized patients with cellulitis, implementation of an evidence-based guideline reduced the average duration of antibiotic use by 3 days, reduced inappropriate use of broad-spectrum antibiotics from 66% to 36%, reduced referrals and imaging, and did not adversely affect cure rates or clinical outcomes. The guideline specifically discouraged use of ESR, superficial wound cultures, CT/MRI, and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Patients were treated empirically with IV vancomycin, NSAIDs, and elevation of the affected limb.

A randomized controlled tiral of an electronic clinical decision support tool (WISCA) for antimicrobial stewardship showed significantly decreased length of hospital stay for patients in the cellulitis subgroup for which IV cefazolin was recommended as first-line (coefficient estimate 0.53).
With early intervention, the prognosis is excellent as most cases of cellulitis resolve with appropriate antibiotic treatment. The infection rarely extends into deeper soft tissues. C

Time to clinical response in uncomplicated cellulitis was 1.68 days in a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Specifically, there was a 33% reduction in area of erythema by day 2-3, a 30-50% decrease in the proportion of patients with edema by day 2-4, and about a 50% reduction in pain and severity score by day 5. B

Although clinical symptoms of leg cellulitis usually improve in the first five days after treatment initiation, over a third of adequately treated patients still have signs and symptoms of inflammation (eg, erythema, edema, warmth, pain) at day 10. In the absence of worsening symptoms, these remaining local symptoms do not indicate treatment failure and are not a reason to prolong or intensify antibiotic therapy. A
Lack of clinical response could be due to unusual organisms, resistant strains of Staphylococcus, a deeper process (ie, necrotizing fasciitis), or misdiagnosis. C
Patients should be advised to watch for systemic symptoms, which may signify complicated or worsening infection. C

The Dundee severity classification divides patients into four classes of increasing severity based on presence or absence of signs of sepsis and underlying comorbidities of peripheral vascular disease, chronic venous insufficiency, and class III obesity. The classification was associated with mortality, length of stay, and readmission in a retrospective cohort study. In a small prospective cohort trial, use of a modified Dundee score identified those of lowest risk of complication (patients categorized as class I were unlikely to have a complicated course (negative LR of 0.12)) and those with the most severe infections (patients categorized as class III or IV had a complicated course (sensitivity 83%, specificity 59%)). B

The mortality rate for hospitalized adults with cellulitis is 0.5% in the USA and 1.1% worldwide. Only one third of deaths appear to be from infection. This mortality rate is comparable to the mortality rate for patients with community-acquired pneumonia who are recommended for outpatient management, suggesting shifts to increased outpatient management for cellulitis may be reasonable and should be studied, including use of severity scores. B

A significant proportion of patients with cellulitis will develop a recurrence within a year. An eight-variable validated Baseline Recurrence Risk in Cellulitis (BRRISC) score has modest performance for identifying risk for recurrence in patients within 90 days of hospitalization for cellulitis ranging from low risk (3.2%) to high risk (16.6%) with points based on age, heart rate, urea, platelets, albumin, previous cellulitis, venous insufficiency, and liver disease. Cluster analysis showed four distinct high-risk groups: (1) acutely ill, younger persons with liver disease; (2) persons with both venous insufficiency and previous cellulitis; (3) persons with severe, chronic renal disease; and (4) severely acutely ill persons with inflammatory responses. B
